title: A reading that never happened
prompt:
The cuff failed on the second reading, so there's no value for it. R
writes a missing value as `NA`.

```r
sbp <- c(118, NA, 131, 156)
class(sbp)
```

What does the last line return?
hint:
In the last module, one text value turned the whole vector to text. Does
`NA` do the same thing?

options.feedback:
Right, and this is worth noticing. `NA` isn't text and it isn't a
word — it's a blank that takes on whatever type the vector already
is. So unlike `"131"` in the last module, a missing value doesn't
drag everything else along with it. The vector is still numbers,
with a hole in it.

That's what a quoted value like `\"131\"` would have done. `NA`
behaves differently: it has no type of its own, so it fits into a
numeric vector without changing it.

On its own, `NA` is technically logical — but once it's inside a
vector of numbers it takes that vector's type. The vector stays
numeric.

options.text: An error — you can't mix `NA` with numbers
options.feedback:
`NA` is allowed anywhere. R is built around the idea that real data is often incomplete, so missing values are a normal part of a vector
rather than a fault.

title: Arithmetic with a hole in it
prompt:
The cuff was reading 10 mmHg high again. What does the last line return?

```r
sbp <- c(118, NA, 131, 156)
sbp - 10
```
hint:
The subtraction still happens to every value. What's ten less than a
number nobody wrote down?

options.feedback:
Yes. The subtraction is applied to every value, exactly as before —
and ten less than an unknown number is still unknown, so the missing value stays missing. `NA` moving through a calculation untouched is the
single most important thing about it.

Only the missing value is affected. The other three are perfectly
good numbers and R subtracts from them normally.

R never quietly drops a value. You get four answers for four
readings, and the one it couldn't work out stays `NA`. Silently
returning three values where you expected four would be far more
dangerous.

That would be treating the missing value as a zero. `NA` doesn't mean zero —
it means nobody knows. Ten less than "nobody knows" is still
"nobody knows".

title: Averaging with a missing value
prompt:
What does this return?

```r
sbp <- c(118, NA, 131, 156)
mean(sbp)
```
hint:
You saw what happened when one value became unknown in the last
exercise.

options.feedback:
Right. One unknown value anywhere in the input makes the answer
unknown, so the whole average comes back `NA`. R is refusing to
guess — and it's refusing loudly enough that you can't miss it,
which is the point.

options.text: `135` — the average of the three real readings
options.feedback:
That's a reasonable answer to a different question, and you can ask
R for it — the next exercise does. But by default, `mean()` includes
every value, missing ones included.

No error — `mean()` returns a value, and the value is `NA`. That's
the quiet kind of failure: it looks like an answer.

options.text: `101.25` — counting the missing value as zero
options.feedback:
That would mean treating a reading nobody took as a reading of
zero. R won't do that, and neither should anyone else.

title: Averaging what you do have
prompt:
You've decided you want the average of just the readings that were
recorded, leaving out the missing one. `mean()` has an argument for
exactly this.

Its usage line is:

```
mean(x, trim = 0, na.rm = FALSE, ...)
```
hint: `na.rm` is short for "NA remove". Its default is `FALSE`.

solution.why:
`na.rm = TRUE` tells `mean()` to drop the missing values before
averaging. The decision is recorded in the code, where anyone reading
it can see what you chose — which is better than a number that quietly
ignored a missing value.

checks.on_fail:
Not 135 yet. The argument that drops missing values needs to be
named and set to `TRUE`.

misconceptions.feedback:
This is why naming matters. The second position in `mean()` is
`trim`, not `na.rm` — look at the usage line again. R takes your
`TRUE` as a value for `trim` and never hears about the missing
value. Write `na.rm = TRUE` and the position stops mattering.

Inside a call you attach a value to an argument with `=`, not `<-`.
`<-` stores something in a variable that lives on afterwards; `=`
says *this value is for that argument, in this call only*.

Still `NA`, so the missing value is still being included. Check the
argument name and that it's set to `TRUE`.

title: Asking which one is missing
prompt:
It seems reasonable to ask which value is the missing one. What does this
return?

```r
sbp <- c(118, NA, 131, 156)
sbp == NA
```
hint:
`==` asks *is this equal to that*. Can you know whether an unknown number
equals an unknown number?

options.feedback:
Yes, and it catches nearly everyone. `==` asks whether two things
are equal, and nobody can say whether a number equals an unknown —
so every answer is itself unknown. Even `118 == NA` is `NA`, not
`FALSE`.

The dangerous part is that this *looks* like it worked. You get four
answers back and none of them is an error. The next exercise has the
function you actually want.

That's the answer you wanted, and it's what `is.na()` gives you —
but `==` can't produce it. Comparing anything with `NA` gives `NA`,
including `NA == NA`.

R doesn't decide the comparison is false. It decides it can't be
answered, which is a different thing and comes back as `NA`.

No error. That's the problem — this runs cleanly and gives you four
useless answers.

title: The function that does work
prompt:
R has a function for this: `is.na()`. It asks each value whether it's
missing, and gives you `TRUE` or `FALSE` for each one.

Use it on `sbp`.
hint: It takes the vector, the same way `class()` did.

solution.why:
`is.na()` is the only reliable way to find missing values. It gives one
answer per value, like every other question you've asked a vector —
and unlike `==`, its answers are never `NA` themselves.

checks.on_fail:
That didn't give one TRUE or FALSE per reading, with the TRUE in
second place.

misconceptions.feedback:
That's `sbp == NA` again. Comparison can't answer this; you need the
function built for it.

title: How much is missing?
prompt: Count how many of the readings are missing.
hint:
`is.na(sbp)` gives `FALSE TRUE FALSE FALSE`. In arithmetic, `TRUE` counts
as 1 and `FALSE` counts as 0. Which function would add those up?

solution.why:
Read it from the inside out. `is.na(sbp)` asks *which values are
missing?* and answers `FALSE TRUE FALSE FALSE`. Wrapping `sum()`
around it asks *how many values are missing in total?* — and since
each TRUE counts as 1, adding them up counts the TRUEs.

When a result comes out strange, this is one of the first things worth
checking.

checks.on_fail: Not 1 yet. You want a function that adds up the TRUEs.

misconceptions.feedback:
`length()` gives 4 — one answer per reading, not the number of
missing ones. Worth knowing on its own, though: `length(sbp)` is
also 4, because a missing value still takes up a place in the vector. The
number of readings you actually have is a different question.

title: Filtering with a missing value
prompt:
This is the filtering you did at the end of the last module, on a vector
that now has a missing value in it.

First, `sbp > 140` gives `FALSE NA FALSE TRUE`. The missing reading can't
be compared with 140, so its answer is `NA` — just as `NA - 10` was `NA`.

```r
sbp <- c(118, NA, 131, 156)
sbp[sbp > 140]
```

What does the last line return?
hint:
Square brackets keep a value where the answer is TRUE and drop it where
the answer is FALSE. What can they do with an `NA`?

options.feedback:
Yes — and this is the one to remember from this module. Square
brackets keep a value wherever the answer is TRUE and drop it
wherever it's FALSE. When the answer is `NA`, they can't decide
either way — so instead of skipping it, they hand back an `NA`.

You asked for readings over 140 and got back a value that was never
a reading at all. Nothing warned you. Count what came back and you
get a clean, wrong answer:

```r
length(sbp[sbp > 140])
```

That returns `2`. There was one high reading.

That's what you wanted, but it isn't what square brackets give you.
They can only keep or drop a value when the answer is TRUE or
FALSE — an `NA` in the question becomes an `NA` in the answer.

The filter does work for the values it can decide about. Only the
missing one causes trouble.

No error. It returns something that looks like a result, which is
exactly what makes it dangerous.

title: Filter without the phantom
prompt:
Now use it. Keep only the readings that aren't missing, then filter what's
left.
hint: The blank is the question you just checked in the last exercise.

solution.why:
`clean` holds the three readings that exist, and filtering those gives
a single answer with nothing invented. Doing it in two steps also
leaves a record: anyone reading this can see that a missing value was
dropped on purpose.

checks.on_fail: `clean` should hold the three readings that aren't missing.
The last line should give just the readings over 140, with no `NA`.

misconceptions.feedback:
You've kept only the missing value instead of everything but it.
`is.na(sbp)` is TRUE where the values are missing — put `!` in front to turn
the question around.

That gives the right answer — for these four readings, and no
others. Give it the next shift's readings and the TRUEs and FALSEs
would be in the wrong places, quietly keeping the wrong values.
`!is.na(sbp)` asks the question fresh every time, whatever the data
turns out to be. Write the question, not its answer.

`clean` is still the original vector, missing value and all, so the `NA` comes
straight through to the answer. The brackets need a question in
them.

title: A missing value is not a zero
prompt:
Three patients were weighed. The second one's weight was never recorded.

Someone building the spreadsheet typed `0` in the empty cell, so the
column reads `70, 0, 82`. Another version left it as `70, NA, 82`.

Both give you a mean. Which one should you report?
hint:
Work out both averages. One of them describes a patient who doesn't
exist.

options.feedback:
Right. This is the average of the patients you actually weighed. It
isn't perfect — you're assuming the missing patient is roughly like
the others — but the assumption is visible in the code, and the
number is one you can defend.

This treats an unrecorded weight as a patient weighing nothing, and
the average drops by 25 kg. Nothing in R can catch this, because `0`
is a perfectly good number. Only someone who knows that adults don't
weigh zero would notice — and that's you.

`na.rm = TRUE` only removes values that are `NA`. To R, a zero isn't
missing — it's a measurement of nothing — so it stays in, and the
average is still 25 kg too low. Once someone has typed a zero into an
empty cell, no argument can tell it apart from a real zero. Only you
can.

This gives `NA`, not a weight. Keeping the missing value as `NA` is the right
instinct — but without `na.rm = TRUE`, `mean()` includes it, and one
unknown value makes the whole average unknown. Easy to forget, and
the reason the argument is worth checking every time you average
something that might have missing values.

title: Where did the answer go?
prompt:
This was meant to store the average and then show it. Press **Run** and
you'll see R report that it can't find `mean_sbp`.

Click the name that actually was created.
hint: Read both names one character at a time.

options.feedback:
Right. The capital `M` makes this a different name entirely, so the
average is sitting safely in `Mean_sbp` while the last line asks for
something that was never created.

Notice that the second line gave no output and no complaint. Storing
something never prints anything, so there was nothing to tell you
the name wasn't the one you meant. The error only appeared one line
later, asking for a name that doesn't exist.

This is the name R can't find — it's the line reporting the problem,
not the line that caused it. Compare it letter by letter with the
name on the line above.

title: Check the question first
prompt:
To get rid of that phantom `NA`, you'll want to keep only the readings
that *aren't* missing. Before you put a question inside square brackets,
it's worth checking what it gives back.

`!` means *not*. What does the last line return?

```r
sbp <- c(118, NA, 131, 156)
!is.na(sbp)
```
hint:
`is.na(sbp)` gives `FALSE TRUE FALSE FALSE`. What does "not" do to each of
those?

options.feedback:
Right. `is.na(sbp)` asks *which values are missing?* Putting `!` in
front turns the question around: *which values are **not**
missing?* Every TRUE becomes FALSE and every FALSE becomes TRUE.

That's exactly the pattern you want inside the brackets — TRUE for
the three readings to keep, FALSE for the missing one. And you know it's
right because you checked before using it.

That's `is.na(sbp)` on its own. The `!` in front turns every answer
around, so TRUE becomes FALSE and FALSE becomes TRUE.

That's where this is heading, but it's one step further on. On its
own, `!is.na(sbp)` gives you TRUEs and FALSEs — the question's
answers. Getting the readings themselves means putting it inside
square brackets, which is the next exercise.
